questions.prompt: Why is the product of two rational expressions a rational expression?
questions.prompt_markup: Why is the product of two rational expressions a rational expression?

choices.text: Rational expressions are always polynomials, and a product of polynomials is a polynomial.
(a/b)(c/d) = (a + c)/(b + d), and a + c and b + d are polynomials, so the product is a ratio of polynomials.
The product of any two expressions is a polynomial.
(a/b)(c/d) = ac/(bd), and ac and bd are polynomials (bd is not the zero polynomial), so the product is a ratio of polynomials.

questions.correct_answer: (a/b)(c/d) = ac/(bd), and ac and bd are polynomials (bd is not the zero polynomial), so the product is a ratio of polynomials.
questions.grading_note: Polynomials are closed under multiplication. The others use an invalid rule or false statements (1/x is not a polynomial).

questions.prompt: Why is the quotient of a rational expression by a nonzero rational expression a rational expression?
questions.prompt_markup: Why is the quotient of a rational expression by a nonzero rational expression a rational expression?

choices.text: Any quotient is undefined, so the question does not apply.
(a/b) ÷ (c/d) = (a ÷ c)/(b ÷ d), and quotients of polynomials are polynomials.
(a/b) ÷ (c/d) = ad/(bc), a ratio of polynomials, and bc is not the zero polynomial because c is not.

questions.correct_answer: (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = ad/(bc), a ratio of polynomials, and bc is not the zero polynomial because c is not.
questions.grading_note: Multiply by the reciprocal. The others claim polynomials are closed under division (they are not) or give non-reasons.

questions.prompt: Which example shows that polynomials are NOT closed under division?
questions.prompt_markup: Which example shows that polynomials are NOT closed under division?

choices.text: 6x² ÷ 3x = 2x for x ≠ 0, which is a polynomial
(x³ + x) ÷ x = x² + 1 for x ≠ 0, a polynomial
x ÷ (x + 1) = x/(x + 1), which is not a polynomial

questions.correct_answer: x ÷ (x + 1) = x/(x + 1), which is not a polynomial
questions.grading_note: One quotient that is not a polynomial is enough. The other quotients are polynomials, so they do not show the failure of closure.
